units: % escape response probability to a simulated approaching predator (mean over all treatments)

source.authors: Zahra M. Bagheri, Callum G. Donohue, Julian C. Partridge, Jan M. Hemmi
source.title: Behavioural and neural responses of crabs show evidence for selective attention in predator avoidance

method: behavioural: escape response of crabs in the field-like arena to computer-generated dark looming disks (single or paired), scored for response probability and timing; treatment order by Latin square
conditions: Wild fiddler crabs collected from intertidal mudflats near Broome, Western Australia and housed at the University of Western Australia; behavioural experiments used 50 crabs (25 females, 25 males) (the Methods sentence also lists 23 crabs for the intracellular experiments). Stimuli were 30 mm dark disks on a collision course approaching at 200 mm/s from 5000 mm, at -100% Weber contrast in Experiment 1 and -40% and -100% in Experiment 2; stimuli single or paired (paired disks separated by 90 or 180 degrees); a stationary grey horizontal bar kept the eyes aligned; at least 3 min acclimatisation and at least 3 min between stimuli; to avoid habituation each crab was exposed to only two stimuli on any given day and tested only every second day, and presentation order was randomized by a Latin square with crabs as columns and treatments as rows, so each crab saw the treatments over several test days. The 75.4% is the average across all treatments, not a threshold; the paper reports that in Experiment 1 response probability and timing did not differ between treatments (one versus two predators, 90 versus 180 degree separation), and that responses to the low-contrast stimulus occurred significantly later (p = 0.004). Response probability did not differ between treatments in Experiment 1 (p = 0.32; timing p = 0.37) or in Experiment 2 (contrast or single versus paired, p = 0.71). Stimulus order had a small but significant positive relationship with escape probability (p = 0.006) and escape timing (p = 0.001). The paper does not give the number of trials or how the 50 crabs were split between the two experiments.
where: Results, Behaviour, Response timing and probability
quote: The crabs reliably responded to all simulated predator treatments with an average response probability of 75.4%.
